lead: Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension. Steel is strong in both. Put steel bars where concrete would crack, and the two materials carry a beam together. That partnership only works if you know how each material behaves when squeezed and stretched. Their stress–strain curves supply every number a design method needs: strength, stiffness, and the strain at which each material gives up. This chapter reads those two curves, defines fck and fy, and adds the time-dependent effects — creep and shrinkage — that change the picture over the life of a structure.
prereq: You need: stress, strain and Hooke's law from engineering mechanics.

sections.h3: Concrete: cube strength and the stress–strain curve

blocks.text: Concrete is cement, fine aggregate, coarse aggregate and water. The cement paste hardens and glues the aggregates into a stony mass. Its useful property is compressive strength. Its tensile strength is only about one-tenth of that, so reinforcing steel is placed to take the tension.

Strength is measured on a 150 mm cube cured 28 days and crushed in a compression testing machine. The grade is written M20, M25 and so on: M stands for mix, and the number is the characteristic cube strength fck in N/mm² at 28 days. IS 456 asks for M20 as the minimum grade for reinforced concrete in mild exposure. Moderate exposure needs M25, and the requirement rises with the severity of exposure.

fck is a characteristic value: only 5% of well-made test cubes are expected to fall below it. A standard cylinder, 150 mm diameter and 300 mm high, gives about 0.8 times the cube strength, because the platens of the machine restrain a cube and make it look stronger. The 5% rule is what 'characteristic' means: the value is a statistical lower bound, not the average strength of the cubes.

The stress–strain curve in compression is not a straight line. Stress climbs steeply, bends over, peaks near a strain of 0.002 at a stress of the order of the cylinder strength, then falls as the concrete cracks. IS 456 keeps 0.0035 as the maximum useful compressive strain in bending. Stiffness is quoted as one secant modulus from zero to the service stress:

blocks.where: Ec is the short-term modulus of elasticity of concrete in N/mm²; fck is the characteristic cube strength in N/mm². For M25, Ec = 5000 × 5 = 25,000 N/mm².

sections.h3: Reinforcing steel: grades and the yield plateau

blocks.text: Steel bars are hot-rolled and ribbed so that concrete grips them. They are graded by characteristic yield strength fy in N/mm²: Fe415, Fe500 and Fe550. Fe is the chemical symbol for iron. Fe415 means a reinforcing bar with characteristic yield strength fy = 415 N/mm²; it does not mean the design stress is 415 N/mm².

Every grade shares one elastic modulus, Es = 2 × 10⁵ N/mm², about eight times the modulus of concrete. The curve is a straight line from zero to yield, so the yield strain is fy/Es. For Fe415: 415 ÷ 200,000 = 0.002075, about 0.00208.

At yield the curve turns flat. This is the yield plateau: strain grows while stress stays almost constant. After yield the steel strain-hardens up to an ultimate tensile strength that lies above the yield stress, the margin shrinking as the grade rises, then it necks and snaps. The plateau is the reason steel is safe in a beam — the member sags visibly before it breaks.

For design, IS 456 replaces the test curve with a design curve: a straight line from zero to a stress of 0.87fy at strain 0.87fy/Es, then a flat line at 0.87fy. Strain hardening is ignored. The 0.87 already contains the partial safety factor of 1.15 on fy. Bars must also be ductile, so each grade carries a minimum elongation at fracture. Fe415 is more ductile than Fe550. A higher grade gives more strength and needs less bar area, at the cost of that ductility.

Two effects change concrete with time. Creep is the slow gain in strain under a sustained load; the creep coefficient φ is creep strain divided by elastic strain. IS 456 gives φ = 2.2 for load first applied at 28 days, falling to about 1.6 if the load is applied at one year. Shrinkage is drying contraction with no load on the member, of the order of 0.0003 strain. Both are largely irreversible and both add deflection to a slab over the years.

Durability closes the list. Dense, low-permeability concrete keeps water and chloride away from the steel. Cover, water–cement ratio and minimum grade are fixed by the exposure class: a coastal site such as Chennai needs more cover and a lower water–cement ratio than a dry inland site, because chlorides break down the passive film on the bars, the steel rusts, swells and splits the concrete.

These numbers set the limits for every method in this unit. The stress block is built from the 0.0035 and 0.002 strains. Partial safety factors are applied to fck and fy, never to Ec. The balanced section of Unit 2 is the one where steel yields at the same instant the concrete reaches 0.0035.

items: Creep coefficient φ = 2.2 for load first applied at 28 days; about 1.6 at one year.
Steel modulus Es = 2 × 10⁵ N/mm² for all grades.

figure.caption: Concrete bends over, peaks near 25 N/mm² and softens; steel climbs in a straight line to 415 N/mm² and then holds a flat plateau. Both events sit close to a strain of 0.002, which is why the two curves are read together.

spec.aria: A plot with a curved concrete stress–strain line peaking near 25 N/mm² and a steel line rising to a flat plateau at 415 N/mm².

examples.question: A simply supported slab uses M25 concrete and Fe415 steel. (a) Estimate the short-term modulus of the concrete. (b) Find the strain at which the steel first yields, taking Es = 2 × 10⁵ N/mm². (c) State the compressive strain in the concrete at peak stress.
steps: Characteristic cube strength of M25 concrete: fck = 25 N/mm².
Characteristic yield strength of Fe415 steel: fy = 415 N/mm².
Yield strain: εy = fy / Es = 415 ÷ 200,000 = 0.002075, about 0.00208.
Concrete reaches peak stress at a strain of about 0.002; its ultimate useful strain in bending is 0.0035.
Check the ratio: Ec/Es = 25,000 ÷ 200,000 = 0.125, so concrete is about one-eighth as stiff as steel.
examples.answer: Ec = 25,000 N/mm², steel yield strain = 0.002075 (about 0.00208), and concrete peak-stress strain ≈ 0.002.
examples.check:
import math
fck = 25
Ec = 5000*math.sqrt(fck)
print(Ec)
fy = 415
Es = 2e5
print(fy/Es)
print(0.002)

traps: Do not treat the cube strength 25 N/mm² as the modulus; Ec is about 25,000 N/mm², a thousand times larger. The unit is N/mm² in both cases, which hides the slip.

415 N/mm² is the characteristic yield strength of Fe415, not the design strength. The design value comes from dividing the characteristic value by a partial safety factor, as the limit state chapter shows.
Cylinder strength is about 0.8 times cube strength. Mixing the two in one calculation is a common examiner's trap and gives answers that are 25% off.
Concrete has no straight elastic portion. Ec = 5000√fck is a secant modulus at service stress, so Hooke's law must not be used up to the peak.
0.0035 is the ultimate compressive strain in bending, not the strain at peak stress; 0.002 is the peak.

quiz.a: The characteristic cube strength: the 28-day compressive strength of 150 mm cubes, in N/mm², below which not more than 5% of test results are expected to fall.

quiz.q: What is fy for Fe500 steel?
Why is a cylinder weaker than a cube of the same concrete?
quiz.a: The platens of the testing machine restrain the cube at its faces, which adds confinement and raises the apparent strength. A cylinder, taller than it is wide, fails in a freer mode, giving about 0.8 times the cube value.

quiz.q: Why does steel show a yield plateau but concrete does not?
quiz.a: Yielding is a slip process inside the metal — planes slide at constant stress — so strain grows with no extra load. Concrete cracks and crumbles progressively, so its curve peaks and then falls.

quiz.q: Find the yield strain of Fe550 steel with Es = 2 × 10⁵ N/mm².
A slab is redesigned from Fe415 to Fe550 steel, keeping the same ultimate moment. What changes and what must be watched?
quiz.a: The required steel area falls roughly in the ratio 415/550, about 0.75 times. But strain at yield rises from 0.00208 to 0.00275, so the section becomes less under-reinforced and less ductile. The designer must recheck minimum steel, spacing and crack control, and development length in Unit 3.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice the stress–strain curve of concrete is now measured directly on cylinders with a compressometer, and high-strength concretes above M60 do not follow the IS 456 parabola at all. Research on fibre-reinforced and self-compacting concrete shows a much flatter falling branch, which matters for seismic design where toughness is wanted. Steel has moved to quenched-and-self-tempered bars and to corrosion-resistant variants for coastal work.
